The Ancient of Days: the lower compasses panel

The frontispiece, the figure with compasses, and why the exact Blake copy matters.

The lower central panel of the compasses cover is identified as a detail of William Blake’s The Ancient of Days by Frank G. Bosman’s cover study. The complete composition supplies context that is lost when the hand and instrument are isolated.

[Image: Lower central panel of the preserved cover, with two golden compass legs extending upward from a hand]
Lower central panel, shown as a cropped view of the preserved cover. The compass legs extend upward in the collage. Compare the hand and rays around it with the complete frontispiece before interpreting this orientation. Open the complete original JPEG.

What is a frontispiece?

A frontispiece is an illustration placed at the beginning of a book. The British Museum’s record for Europe: a Prophecy, copy A, plate 1 identifies this design as its frontispiece. The catalogue describes a bearded figure in a luminous sphere, extending compasses into the darkness below. It gives the figure’s identity as probably Urizen; that qualification should remain when citing the record.

The collection record describes a particular copy. A work title alone does not identify which impression, colouring or modern reproduction was used in the puzzle image. This entry does not establish that the collage was made from the museum’s copy A.

Which museum object is linked?
	Catalogue field	British Museum record
	Registration number	1936,1116.32
	Work and position	Europe: a Prophecy, copy A, plate 1
	Production	1794; published in London
	Process and ink	Relief and white-line etching, printed in blue-green ink
	Catalogued dimensions	234 × 168 mm
The museum’s curator notes describe copy A as an early, incomplete proof: eleven plates on eight leaves, with almost no hand-colouring. They separately give approximate sheet dimensions of 332 × 262 mm. These are physical dimensions, not pixel sizes for a downloaded image.
The registration number identifies this collection object; its opening year is not the work’s production date. Keep the copy, plate, date, and physical dimensions attached to their catalogue labels when taking notes.
Why the copy matters to the cover comparison
The blue-green proof provides a reference for the composition, while the preserved cover fragment has a different colour appearance. That difference leaves an exact source-copy identification open. It could require comparison with other impressions or reproductions, as well as any changes made while assembling the collage. The linked record alone does not decide between those possibilities.
A useful comparison record names both images, marks corresponding contours, and records any crop, rotation, reflection, or colour adjustment. Matching the hand and instrument can support identification of the design. Identifying one particular reproduction requires finer evidence, such as matching print detail or image defects. Use original-image coordinates to make those comparisons inspectable.
How to compare the cover

Open the original cover and the museum’s complete design.
Trace the hand and the two legs of the instrument. Compare their relationship to the surrounding light and the partly visible head.
Check the orientation: Bosman describes a rotated fragment. Record the rotation and crop separately instead of treating a transformed image as a different drawing.
To identify an exact source copy, compare small distinctive details and colour placement across documented copies, not merely the common outline.

The name in Daniel 7

The phrase appears in Daniel 7:9–14, here linked in the King James Version. This is a judgment scene in a vision, distinct from Nebuchadnezzar’s episode in chapter 4.

Verses 9–10
The Ancient of Days is seated, with white clothing and hair compared to wool. The throne, wheels, and a stream are described through fire. A multitude attends, judgment is set, and books are opened.
Verses 13–14
A figure described as like the Son of man approaches with the clouds and comes before the Ancient of Days. Dominion and an enduring kingdom are granted.

These verses supply a location for the name and its surrounding imagery. They do not describe a figure extending compasses from a luminous sphere. That distinction matters when moving from a title to the details of Blake’s composition.

A biblical title and a Blake character

Keep the title’s textual background separate from the identification of the figure. The museum record above calls the figure probably Urizen; the Urizen guide explains that character’s role in Blake. Neither label makes the frontispiece a literal illustration of every detail in Daniel’s vision.

Bosman’s cover interpretation brings the title and Nebuchadnezzar together through Daniel. Readers can now inspect both passages directly. This is a checkable literary connection, but it still leaves the puzzle authors’ purpose and any proposed book-cipher operation to be demonstrated separately.

What the repeated instrument tells us

Newton, in the upper panel, also supplies a hand with compasses. The collage therefore places two acts of measurement together. Reading that arrangement as a theme is different from extracting a key from it: a cipher proposal needs an explicit rule that someone else can apply to the same source bytes.

See Nebuchadnezzar for the side panels and the proposed Daniel connection, and William Blake and Liber Primus for the manuscript’s textual allusion.


For the terminology behind these comparisons, see Blake prints: plates, impressions, and copies. Its illustrated explanation separates the printing method from the identity of a particular source image.

Decrypting the illustrated cover’s RSA message

Reproduce the three historical RSA blocks and understand the Crypt::RSA 1.99 padding difference.

The 1033.jpg cover hides a signed message containing an RSA public key and encrypted data. This guide reproduces the historical decryption using published factors. It recovers a navigation address from the 2014 puzzle; it does not solve an unknown manuscript page.

Run the reproduction

Extract the reference-data ZIP. From the extracted folder, run:

python scripts/reproduce_cover_rsa.py

The script needs only Python 3’s standard library. It reads the included verified message body and makes no network requests. Its output lists three blocks, their recovered bytes and successful RSA round-trip checks. The complete plaintext is:

\ncu343l33nqaekrnw.onion\n\n

Here \n denotes a newline byte. The address is historical output, not a service contacted by this reproduction. Download the recorded result or inspect the script.

What the key numbers mean

The signed body gives e = 65537 and a modulus n. The modulus is the integer that defines the range of RSA arithmetic; this one is 432 bits long. The public exponent e specifies the public modular-power operation. To undo it, this reproduction uses two published factors, p and q, whose product equals n.

Connor Tumbleson’s reconstruction supplies those factors. The script checks their product against the modulus read from the message, calculates phi = (p - 1)(q - 1), and obtains the private exponent as the modular inverse d = e⁻¹ mod phi. Supplying the factors avoids repeating factor discovery. The fast runtime of this script therefore says nothing about how long factoring took.

For a small worked example of that calculation, see the totient and RSA. It explains why the factors must be distinct primes and how a modular inverse differs from division.

Unwrap the message in the right order

Base64: decode the printable encrypted block into bytes.
Checksum: compare the attached MD5 value with the compressed bytes. This is the historical format’s integrity check, not a substitute for the PGP signature.
Compression: decompress the zlib stream.
Content frame: read the length-prefixed field named Cyphertext, preserving that spelling. It holds 162 bytes: three 54-byte RSA blocks.
RSA: for each ciphertext integer c, calculate m = cᵈ mod n. Re-encrypt m and require the original c.
Padding: decode the legacy OAEP structure and concatenate the three recovered message fragments.

Why an ordinary OAEP decoder can fail

OAEP adds structured padding before RSA encryption. Recovering the modular integer is only part of decryption; the padding must also be decoded using the same rules as the sender.

The message names Crypt::RSA::ES::OAEP, version 1.99. In that release’s DataFormat.pm, the SHA-1 mask generator uses counters 0, 20, 40 and so on. Standard MGF1 advances by one instead. This small implementation difference changes the mask bytes and causes a standard decoder to reject this message’s padding. The reproduction follows the named legacy implementation and checks the empty-label hash and padding delimiter in every block.

On 20 October 2026, a separate PyCryptodome 3.23.0 OAEP decoder with the legacy mask rule matched all three fragments. Its default mask rejected all three. This is a compatibility finding about this historical message, not a reason to use these old rules for new encryption.

Sources and scope

Input: the extracted message body, with its hash checked before decoding. Signature and extraction evidence: cover provenance. Implementation reference: Crypt::RSA 1.99 source archive, especially DataFormat.pm and ES/OAEP.pm. The result record includes the archive checksum and block-level outputs.

The complete path is now OutGuess extraction, signature verification, then this RSA replay. These operations establish different things: recovered carrier bytes, a valid signed message, and a matching historical plaintext.

Emerson’s Self-Reliance and the opening book cipher

The essay’s documented place in the 2014 route, a first-coordinate example, and comparisons with Liber Primus.

Ralph Waldo Emerson’s Self-Reliance belongs in the history of the 2014 puzzle for a specific reason: the archived opening route uses it as a book-cipher source. It also offers useful comparisons with Liber Primus’s treatment of inward knowledge and conformity. Those are two different connections, with different kinds of evidence.

Its place before the illustrated cover

The pinned 2014 walkthrough identifies Emerson’s essay as the source indicated by the opening riddle. It records a four-part lookup rule: paragraph, sentence, word, letter. The reported result is auqgnxjtvdbll3pv.onion, the historical site that displayed the 1033.jpg compasses collage.

This places the essay before the cover’s RSA message. The two addresses belong to successive steps; they are not conflicting solutions to the same clue. Neither address is contacted by the site’s reproduction scripts.

Follow the first coordinate

The walkthrough points to this Dartmouth-hosted PDF of Self-Reliance. The first coordinate is 1:2:3:1. Count from the first prose paragraph, after the title and opening verse. Its second sentence begins The soul always. The third word is always, whose first letter is a. This agrees with the first character of the reported address.

Reproduce all the lookups

The complete replay was checked on 20 October 2026. Extract the reference-data ZIP and run:

python scripts/reproduce_emerson.py

This uses Python’s standard library and the included paragraph derivative. It prints the complete result and every selected sentence, word and character. The output is auqgnxjtvdbll3pv.onion; no network request is made.

For a second level of reproduction, install pypdf==6.19.0 in your Python environment and run python scripts/reproduce_emerson.py --check-pdf. This re-extracts the included source PDF and compares all 50 derived paragraphs before doing the lookups. The default command does not require that package.

The counting rules used here

Counting starts at the first prose paragraph and excludes the title, opening verse and page-number footers. Sentences end at periods, question marks or exclamation marks. Words are separated by whitespace, with punctuation removed from their edges; only alphabetic characters count within the selected word. All coordinates start at 1. Typographical ligatures are expanded, and words split with a line-ending hyphen are joined while retaining the hyphen.

One detail changes the later paragraph numbers: the two inset verse lines on printed page 16 stay within paragraph 36. They are not two additional prose paragraphs. An initial automatic extraction counted them separately; inspecting the PDF explained the resulting mismatches. This is a documented correction during replay of a known result, not an independently predicted decoding rule.

The full evidence record contains source and derivative checksums, every coordinate and selected sentence, and the conventions. The paragraph derivative records the printed starting page for each paragraph. The coordinates are now read directly from the freshly extracted and signature-verified opening message. The script checks the body checksum and coordinate sequence before replaying them. It also does not establish that the PDF snapshot is byte-for-byte the edition originally used by the puzzle authors.

What “self-reliance” means in the essay

Read the essay in Emerson’s Essays, First Series, under Self-Reliance. Emerson’s instruction to Trust thyself concerns confidence in one’s own judgment rather than dependence on social approval. His argument against conformity questions obedience to inherited opinion. These are claims about how to think and live, not a set of cipher instructions.

There are useful points of comparison with Liber Primus’s final LP1 instruction, which directs attention inward, and The Loss of Divinity, which examines adherence and the desire to belong. Read the passages together before calling them equivalent: the manuscript develops its own vocabulary of circumference, divinity and primality.

There is also a tension worth keeping visible. Emerson’s appeal to self-trust does not automatically explain the manuscript’s promised end to self or its koans about identity. The same word can carry different meanings in different arguments. The philosophical themes guide follows those distinctions within Liber Primus.

The dedicated comparison of self, identity and self-trust follows Emerson’s explicit question about the “aboriginal Self” in paragraph 21. It explains why self-trust is more demanding than defending whatever a person already believes, and compares that argument with the two koans.

Three passages to read closely

The locations below use the same 50-paragraph source derivative as the reproduction script. Paragraphs count from one. The printed page is where the paragraph starts in the preserved Dartmouth PDF; these numbers should not be transferred to another edition.

Conformity: paragraph 6, printed page 3

“The virtue in most request is conformity. Self-reliance is its aversion.”

The surrounding passage compares society to a company whose members exchange some independence for security. Emerson’s objection concerns the price of acceptance: a person may surrender judgment to inherited names and customs. This is more specific than a general instruction to be different.

Compare The Loss of Divinity, where adherence is criticized when its motive is belonging and being right. The manuscript explicitly includes both dogma and reason as things a person might follow for that motive. The overlap is a concern about dependence on approval; the wording and surrounding explanations are not identical.

Consistency: paragraph 14, printed page 7

“Speak what you think now in hard words, and to-morrow speak what to-morrow thinks in hard words again, though it contradict every thing you said to-day.”

This follows Emerson’s famous criticism of a “foolish consistency.” The practical issue is whether loyalty to an earlier statement prevents a person from expressing a present conviction. Read the paragraph rather than reducing the phrase to permission for arbitrary contradiction.

Liber Primus’s warning directs readers to test knowledge, while also preserving the book’s words and numbers. Those instructions address different objects: a reader’s beliefs may change while the source being examined remains intact. That is an internal comparison with the manuscript, not evidence that this particular Emerson paragraph supplied its wording.

Fortune and inward stability: paragraph 50, printed page 21

“Nothing can bring you peace but yourself. Nothing can bring you peace but the triumph of principles.”

In the preceding sentences, Emerson lists favorable events that can raise someone’s spirits, including a political victory and the return of an absent friend. His conclusion shifts attention from those changing circumstances to the self and principles. It is an argument about where stability is sought, not a claim that outward events never matter.

The manuscript’s discussion of possessions and fear of losing them offers a useful comparison: The Loss of Divinity distinguishes accumulating wealth from attachment to it. Yet Emerson’s concluding self-trust and Liber Primus’s promised end to self should not be flattened into a single teaching. The koans ask what identity means; they do not merely repeat an instruction to trust an already-defined self.

Keep the historical and interpretive claims distinct

	Claim	Evidence available here

	The essay functions as a source in the opening book cipher.	The preserved coordinates, declared counting rules, and reproduced historical output.

	Its arguments can be compared with Liber Primus.	The passages above beside the documented manuscript readings.

	A specific passage intentionally inspired a manuscript sentence.	Not established by thematic resemblance or the book-cipher replay alone.

	The essay provides a key for another page.	Requires a separately specified and tested transformation.


This lets the essay play two useful roles without confusing them: a concrete input in a historical computation, and a text to read alongside the manuscript’s ideas.

A reading edition is not automatically a cipher edition

The Gutenberg text is useful for reading the essay and locating themes. The Dartmouth PDF is the edition linked by the walkthrough. Do not assume that paragraph, sentence or word counts can be transferred between them without comparison. A line break introduced by a PDF page boundary is not necessarily a paragraph break; titles, epigraphs and footnotes can also shift a naïve count.

The historical use of this essay makes it a documented source in the earlier puzzle. It does not establish that Emerson supplies a key to an unsolved LP2 page. Any such proposal needs its own input, selection rule and reproducible test.


For the historical movement around Emerson, see transcendentalism. It supplies context for comparative reading, not an additional demonstrated manuscript source.

Book ciphers: coordinates, editions and counting rules

How text lookups work and what to preserve so another reader can reproduce them.

A book cipher turns coordinates into text by looking them up in a shared source. The source can be an essay, poem or other document; it need not be a whole book. To reproduce a result, knowing the title is not enough. You also need the edition and the rules used to count its parts.

How a four-part lookup works

In a paragraph:sentence:word:letter scheme, 2:1:3:2 means: select paragraph 2, then its first sentence, then its third word, then the second letter of that word. This assumes one-based counting, where the first item is numbered 1.

For a small invented example, let paragraph 2 begin We study runes. The third word is runes, so the second letter is u. The coordinates identify nested locations; they are not numbers to add together.

The archived 2014 opening puzzle uses this kind of rule with Emerson’s Self-Reliance. That guide traces all 15 coordinates and the literal characters against a derivative of the referenced PDF, with downloadable source files and a reproduction script.

Reproduce the small example

The nested lists below explicitly define paragraphs, sentences, and words. That makes the counting visible; this example does not pretend to automatically recognize those boundaries in an arbitrary PDF. The words contain only letters, so character positions and letter positions agree here.

# document[paragraph][sentence][word]
document = [
    [["First", "paragraph"]],
    [["We", "study", "runes"]],
]

def lookup(document, coordinate):
    if len(coordinate) != 4 or any(type(n) is not int or n < 1 for n in coordinate):
        raise ValueError("Use four positive one-based integer coordinates")
    p, s, w, letter = coordinate
    try:
        word = document[p - 1][s - 1][w - 1]
        character = word[letter - 1]
    except IndexError as error:
        raise ValueError(f"Coordinate out of range: {coordinate}") from error
    return word, character

coordinate = (2, 1, 3, 2)
word, character = lookup(document, coordinate)
print(coordinate, word, character)
assert (word, character) == ("runes", "u")
# (2, 1, 3, 2) runes u

The subtraction of 1 converts each published coordinate to Python’s zero-based indexing. Validate positivity before subtracting: an input coordinate of zero would otherwise become index −1, which Python interprets as the last item. An invalid coordinate could silently produce a plausible letter instead of failing.

	Step	Published coordinate	Python index	Selected item

	Paragraph	2	1	Second paragraph

	Sentence	1	0	We study runes

	Word	3	2	runes

	Letter	2	1	u


Decide what counts before extracting

Starting point
State whether titles, opening quotations and notes are included. Starting at the first prose paragraph can differ from starting at the first text on the page.

Paragraph boundaries
Preserve actual paragraph divisions. A page or display line ending may interrupt a paragraph without creating a new one.

Sentence boundaries
Specify how punctuation and abbreviations are handled. Splitting blindly at every period can create false sentences.

Word and letter boundaries
Record how hyphens, apostrophes, punctuation and accented letters are treated. Counting characters in a raw file is not necessarily counting letters in the printed word.

Literal characters
A clue may print some digits or punctuation directly. Identify those separately instead of forcing every item through the coordinate rule.

For example, the raw characters in don't put the apostrophe in position 4 and t in position 5. Counting letters only instead puts t in position 4. Neither convention should be introduced only after seeing which one gives a desired output. Define it for the whole extraction and retain the original spelling.

Why a different edition can change the result

A text with the same title can differ in paragraph divisions, punctuation, added notes, or corrected spelling. In a nested coordinate system, these differences act at different levels: a new paragraph can shift paragraph coordinates, an altered sentence boundary can shift sentence coordinates within that paragraph, and a changed word can affect its letter positions.

A matching PDF checksum establishes that two researchers started from the same file. It does not establish that their PDF-to-text tools produced the same paragraphs. Preserve the extracted derivative and its rules as well as the source file. The Emerson replay provides a concrete example of keeping the source PDF, paragraph data, lookup rule, and output trace together.

What a reproducible trace should show

For each coordinate, record the selected paragraph, sentence, word and letter, plus the resulting output character. Include the source URL, a file checksum, and any transcription changes. A reader should be able to inspect one disagreeing character without rerunning an opaque decoder.

If a coordinate points beyond a sentence or word, report it as out of range. Wrapping around, skipping a heading or switching editions introduces another rule. Such a rule may be worth testing, but it must be stated rather than hidden inside a correction.

Using a possible literary reference

A recognizable quotation or artwork can suggest a source to investigate. It does not identify the indexing scheme. Before trying many passages and counting conventions, write down the source, coordinates, transformations and success criterion. Otherwise a promising fragment may simply be the best-looking result among many undocumented choices.

The experiment-writing guide explains how to preserve that scope. Use Have we tried it? to look for a documented test of the same technique and inputs, rather than treating any mention of the source as evidence that the test was performed.

A complete historical control
The Emerson control experiment records a fresh PDF reconstruction, all 15 coordinate lookups and seven literal characters, exact inputs and two matching reruns. It reproduces the historical opening puzzle, not an unsolved LP2 page. Earlier adjustments to paragraph extraction remain disclosed.

The 2014 opening image and its hidden message

The original zN4h51m.jpg, verified OutGuess content, and the route through Emerson to the compasses cover.

The opening image of the archived 2014 route is a dark JPEG with a greeting, a pilgrimage announcement, a faint insect-like figure and the number 3301. Its archive filename is zN4h51m.jpg. Unlike a numbered Liber Primus page, its role here is to introduce the route that leads to the manuscript.

[Image: Black opening image with white greeting and pilgrimage text, a faint winged figure, a good-luck wish and 3301.]
The unchanged opening JPEG. The faint central image is part of the source, not a loading error.

Download the original JPEG · Provenance and verification evidence

The visible image and hidden message

The visible text announces the beginning of a journey. The hidden OutGuess message supplies something operational: a short riddle, fifteen four-part coordinates, and several literal characters. The Self-Reliance guide shows how those coordinates select letters from Emerson’s essay.

The extraction was reproduced on 20 October 2026 and recovered exactly 1,150 bytes. The clear-signed block verified with GnuPG 2.5.21 against the recorded Cicada fingerprint, in an isolated keyring without a digest-policy override. Signature verification authenticates the signed message against that key; it does not sign the entire JPEG or establish a real-world author.

Full extraction · Signed block · Readable body

Reproduce the extraction and lookup

Extract the reference data and original images into the same folder. With OutGuess installed, run:

python scripts/extract_payload.py opening-2014 --outguess outguess --output opening.bin

The wrapper checks the input JPEG and the recovered output before writing a new file. Expected output: 1,150 bytes with SHA-256 cba64781bd461b17039316ef97426f912aae987fde131f62e883f7f9e9f0118e. It refuses to overwrite an existing file.

Prepare the isolated keyring using the signature guide, then verify the preserved block:

gpg --no-options --homedir verify-keyring --no-auto-key-retrieve --status-fd 1 --verify exports/steganography/opening-2014.signed.asc

The expected VALIDSIG fingerprint is 6D854CD7933322A601C3286D181F01E57A35090F. Next run python scripts/reproduce_emerson.py. That script reads the coordinates from the extracted body, checks its checksum and reproduces every lookup. It does not invoke GnuPG itself.

How the early steps connect

This opening image carries the riddle and coordinates.
The Emerson book cipher yields the historical address where the compasses collage appeared.
The collage contains a different signed message, with RSA parameters and encrypted bytes.
The RSA replay recovers the next historical address using published factors.

These are earlier puzzle artifacts, separate from the 75 numbered manuscript records. The source image is preserved from the pinned community archive; the same archive’s walkthrough documents the route. Reproducing it does not require visiting the historical services.

The two koans: identity and the inner voice

A close reading of the master–student exchanges, their use of circumference, and the limits of a Zen attribution.

Liber Primus labels two sections A Koan. Both stage an exchange between a master and a student, but they ask different questions. The first tests the descriptions a person offers as an identity. The second turns a denial of an inner voice into an example of that voice.

Read the first section, LP1-06–09, and the second section, LP1-14–15, alongside this guide. Their pages, literal readings and decoding instructions are separate from the interpretation offered here.

What is a koan?

In Zen contexts, a kōan can take the form of a puzzling question or encounter used in training. It is not simply a brainteaser whose purpose is to produce a clever verbal answer. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy’s account of Japanese Zen, section 2, places kōan practice within cultivation of wisdom and compassion, and describes its particular role in Rinzai training.

That background helps explain why a master might reject an answer that is factually correct. It does not identify Liber Primus’s dialogues with any particular traditional case. The manuscript gives the genre label but supplies no author, collection, case number or lineage for either story.

Zen, Rinzai, and Sōtō

These names describe a religious and philosophical setting, rather than three kinds of puzzle:

Zen
A Buddhist tradition whose Japanese name comes from Chinese Chán, ultimately related to Sanskrit dhyāna, meditation. The practical setting matters: a dialogue belongs to a wider discipline, not just a collection of clever answers.
Rinzai
A Japanese Zen school particularly associated with organized kōan training and consultation with a teacher.
Sōtō
A Japanese Zen school associated with shikantaza, or “just sitting.” It does not use the same elaborate kōan training system.

This brief distinction follows sections 1–2 of the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy’s account of Japanese Zen (revised 7 March 2024). It introduces the terms; it is not a complete account of either school.

Liber Primus supplies the heading A KOAN and a master–student exchange. It does not name Rinzai, Sōtō, a teacher’s lineage, or a traditional case collection. The useful comparison is therefore at the level of literary form and the questioning of ordinary answers. A stronger attribution would need the specific textual evidence described below.

First koan: what an answer describes

The first student seeks admission to study. Each answer to the master’s identity question changes the kind of description being offered:

	Answer offered	How the master classifies it	What changes in the exchange

	A name	A label used to address the person	The question is separated from naming.

	A profession	An activity or social role	The question is separated from work.

	Being human	Membership in a species	The answer moves from social identity to a biological category.

	Consciousness inhabiting a body	An account of what the person is	Even an abstract account does not satisfy the master’s distinction.


The student eventually begins an answer and cannot complete it. After the pause, the master admits him. The story ends with admission rather than a final definition of the self. One reading is that the student has reached the limits of the descriptions he initially relied on. Another emphasis would be his change from confident answers to uncertainty. Neither reading requires supplying a missing final word as if it were decoded plaintext.

The instruction after the first dialogue
LP1-09 ends the exchange with the master admitting the student. A separate instruction follows: DO-FOUR-UNREASONABLE-THNGS-EACH-DAY, with the manuscript line wraps joined here. On the original sheet, an insect sits between the dialogue and this passage; an enlarged red initial and red heading mark the new opening.
[Image: Lower passage on LP1-09: large red initial and red heading followed by three rows of runic text.]
The closing instruction, original-image rectangle [570, 2370, 1250, 560]. See its position on the complete page · Original JPEG.
Keeping the instruction separate matters: the dialogue does not itself describe four actions, and the instruction does not list which actions to perform. Its possible comparison with the White Queen’s six impossible things belongs in the Carroll guide, which distinguishes the number, action, wording and context. That comparison does not identify the source of the preceding master-and-student story.

Second koan: the denial becomes the example

The second master associates the “I” with the voice of the circumference. A student inwardly denies having such a voice and prepares to object. The master points to the just-formed denial as the example the student was looking for.

The exchange is self-referential: an act of thinking about thought becomes part of the argument. Its effect depends on the narration telling us what this student thought. The story does not establish that every person experiences thought as verbal inner speech, nor does it offer a psychological test of readers.

Its vocabulary also belongs to the surrounding manuscript. The Loss of Divinity assigns consumption, preservation and adherence to the circumference. LP2-57’s parable describes shedding circumferences. Following those uses gives the term more context than treating it immediately as a reference to circles in a diagram.

What does “self-referential” mean here?

The exchange turns back on something happening inside the exchange itself. The master does not answer the student with an unrelated example: he uses the student’s response. The diagram separates the narrated event from the explanation the master attaches to it.

[Image: Three steps: the master describes an inner voice; the student forms an inward denial; the master points to that denial as his example. These are paraphrases, not literal text.]
Argument sequence in LP1-14–15. Open full size · Download the diagram (SVG).

Two questions remain distinct. Did the student have the thought? Within the story, the narrator says so. Does that thought establish the master’s account of the I and circumference? The master treats it that way, but the occurrence of a thought does not by itself explain what those terms mean. A reader can follow the rhetorical move without accepting the whole account.

Self-reference is also not automatically a logical paradox. The scene does not force a statement to be both true and false. It presents a disagreement about what counts as an example. Nor does it show how the master knows the student’s unspoken thought; that is part of the story’s presentation, not a demonstrated ability. Compare testing knowledge and authority for the distinction between an asserted explanation and evidence for it.

How the two stories work together

The first dialogue unsettles what the student can say about himself; the second questions the voice doing the saying. This is a useful internal connection between the stories. It also helps frame the Welcome section’s promised end to self: what is being brought to an end—a person, a description, or a habitual way of identifying oneself? The manuscript’s stories make that question available without settling it through a formal definition.

Compare Emerson’s self-trust with care. The earlier puzzle’s use of Emerson is documented, but “self” need not mean the same thing in every work. Likewise, identifying the stories as koans does not establish that every claim in Liber Primus belongs to Zen doctrine.

Which self should be trusted? Emerson explicitly asks that question in the source essay. The comparison follows his answer alongside the koans’ unfinished identity answer and inner-voice example.

What would establish an outside source?

A source claim needs a specific passage, a traceable edition or translation, and enough shared wording or structure to compare the exchanges in detail. A generic master-and-student story is weak evidence by itself. If a candidate is found, record differences as well as similarities and ask whether the source predates the manuscript.

Keep a literary interpretation separate from a cipher proposal. If “circumference” suggests a key or a reading path, state the exact symbols and transformation, then follow the reproduction requirements. A thematic connection is a reason to investigate; the resulting computation still needs to be checked.

Sources and reading status

The analysis above uses the first koan and second koan in the 5 October 2026 reading snapshot. The Zen reference supplies background, not an attribution of the manuscript. For the wider internal connections, continue with philosophical themes.


Follow the recurring term in circumference, identity, and emergence, or use the known-reading concordance to locate a word or phrase yourself.

The first koan’s bearded-figure frame appears on all four LP1-06–09 sheets. LP1-09 includes an insect before the closing instruction. The visual inventory records those features without identifying the figure as the master in the story.

Dots and punctuation

Compare large dot arrangements, border marks, and small punctuation clusters, with original-image details and page locations.

“Dots” can mean several visibly different things in Liber Primus. Large dots separated by wide spaces, small marks between runes, and compact multi-dot clusters should not be treated as one symbol just because a transcription uses similar punctuation for them.
Five-dot arrangements: where to look
These three pages all contain a group of five large black dots. Their positions relative to the writing differ, so a reference to “the five dots” should include a page ID.
	Page	Location of the dots	Surrounding material
	LP2-07	Below the text	A short red closing line and curled side borders
	LP2-23	Above the text	The opening of the community Mayfly grouping
	LP2-56	Below the text	The An End reading and printed hexadecimal target
This is a location comparison, not a claim that the patterns are identical or encode the same operation. Use each original image for measurements.
LP2-07 has five large black dots beneath its red closing line. They form a loose arrangement rather than one straight row. Smaller specks also appear beside the upper spiral drawings, so “the dots on page 7” should specify which group is meant.
[Image: LP2-07 cropped page preview]
LP2-07 · Read
See spirals and branching borders for the surrounding LP2-03–07 group.
LP2-23 also has five large dots, this time above the text. Their placement differs from the group below the text on LP2-07. A relationship between these arrangements would need a specified comparison; the shared count alone does not establish a code.
[Image: LP2-23: five large dots above the text]
LP2-23 — five large dots above the text. Open reader
Continue with the Mayfly group and insect imagery.
Five dots below the hash-target page · LP2-56
LP2-56 has five large filled black dots below its final two runic rows. Their loose arrangement differs from the compact small punctuation clusters within the writing. The five-row hexadecimal block sits higher on the page, between the runic passages.
[Image: LP2-56 detail: five large black dots in a loose arrangement below the text.]
Original-image detail, rectangle [800, 2350, 900, 500]. Complete page · Original JPEG.
Compare this with the five-dot arrangements on LP2-07 and LP2-23. A shared count is a starting observation; it does not establish the same spacing, orientation or role. A geometric comparison should state the dot centers and transformations used, rather than matching only the number five.
Measure these five dots with the original-image rectangle, a reproducible Python command and a table of pixel areas and centroids.
The hash-target guide explains the printed hexadecimal string and its limits. The known reading is a separate result from an interpretation of the dots: decoding the words does not by itself give the marks a meaning.
Large separated dots
LP2-33 has three conspicuous black dots between two blocks of text. LP2-39 also has a separated row of three dots. These are useful starting points when someone remembers “the page with dots.” This pair is a set of illustrated examples, not an exhaustive dot inventory of all 75 pages.
[Image: Three large separated dots between the text blocks on LP2-33.]
Three large separated dots between the text blocks on LP2-33. Page record · Original JPEG
[Image: Three separated dots within the layout of LP2-39.]
Three separated dots within the layout of LP2-39. Page record · Original JPEG
Solid marks and pale rings on LP2-53

The small clusters beside LP2-53’s curled borders differ in fill. The left cluster has three solid black marks and two pale outlined rings; the right has five solid black marks. A count that treats only dark filled shapes as dots would describe these groups differently from a count that includes rings.

[Image: Left border cluster on LP2-53, with original color and orientation preserved]
Left cluster. Display window: 300, 1400, 200, 200 pixels (x, y, width, height).
[Image: Right border cluster on LP2-53, with original color and orientation preserved]
Right cluster. Display window: 1900, 1400, 200, 200 pixels (x, y, width, height).
These enlarged views use the preserved JPEG; they are not thresholded or recolored. Open the image to inspect the marks in context. The fill difference is an observation, not evidence by itself for a binary code. A proposed extraction needs an explicit ordering, a rule for pale outlines, and a stated set of pages to compare. See image regions and measurement rules.
The same left/right fill pattern is also visible on LP2-40 and LP2-54: three solid marks plus two pale outlines on the left, five solid marks on the right. These are separately inspected examples, not a verified count across the entire border group. Compare their layouts in the group-opening comparison.
Red closing clusters on LP2-22, LP2-32, and LP2-55
These three pages end their black rune text with a narrow red cluster of small square marks. The clusters occupy a similar place in the text layout even though the drawings below them differ: a reclining figure on LP2-22, a soft-edged tree on LP2-32, and a pale tree above a winged figure on LP2-55.
[Image: Red closing cluster from LP2-22, shown with original color and orientation.]
LP2-22
Region: 1600, 1660, 100, 160 pixels.
[Image: Red closing cluster from LP2-32, shown with original color and orientation.]
LP2-32
Region: 900, 1590, 100, 160 pixels.
[Image: Red closing cluster from LP2-55, shown with original color and orientation.]
LP2-55
Region: 1010, 1220, 100, 160 pixels.
The detail views show unchanged regions of the original JPEGs, at the same display scale. Open a page record and choose Inspect Red dotted mark at the end of the text to see its surrounding text. These are selected examples, not a claim that only these pages have red closing marks.
Calling one a “closing cluster” describes its position. It does not determine whether a key resets there, whether it separates sentences or sections, or whether visually similar clusters represent identical instructions. The color-boundary guide explains which additional rules a cipher proposal must specify. The opening-page component counts below apply to their measured regions; they should not be copied onto these examples without measurement.
Small marks and compact clusters
The LP2-00–02 inventory records punctuation separately from rune shapes. Its measured regions include one-, four-, and thirteen-component groups. A “component” is a connected set of dark pixels under a specified threshold. It is not automatically one intentional dot: touching marks can merge, and tiny specks can be excluded.
Published measurements for the opening pages
	Page	Punctuation regions	Recorded groups	Red punctuation
	LP2-00	58	56 × one; 1 × four; 1 × thirteen	One one-component region and the thirteen-component region
	LP2-01	62	57 × one; 5 × four	None under the recorded rule
	LP2-02	38	36 × one; 1 × four; 1 × thirteen	The thirteen-component region
The printed mark and the exported character
In the archive notation, a comma represents a three-dot symbol; a period is a clause separator, and an ampersand is a paragraph separator. These are editorial conventions. They are not instructions to insert the prime value of a comma, reset a key, or skip a rune.
One exported character can stand for visually different marks. Before a punctuation-based experiment, identify the exact image regions and the precise sequence you are testing. Otherwise a result may describe the transcriber’s decisions rather than the printed manuscript.
The LP2-31 row example compares an original row, archive punctuation and expanded Latin labels, with reproducible counts.
Inspect and reproduce
Open an opening-page record and expand “Recorded punctuation regions.”
Use “Inspect region” to compare the stored rectangle against the full image.
Follow the opening-page reproduction instructions to rerun the pixel counts.
For the measurement rules, see image regions and connected components. For archived versus reviewed punctuation, see the punctuation review record. The large-dot examples above have not been assigned a cipher function.

Möbius and the crossed-loop drawing

Find the LP2-15–22 grouping, inspect the loop beneath the number panel, and distinguish the visual name from a geometric claim.

The name Möbius (also written Mobius or Moebius) is used for the LP2-15–22 section. The most recognizable detail is the crossed, two-lobed drawing beneath the numbers on LP2-15. Start there if you remember an infinity-shaped symbol or a number square.
[Image: LP2-15: the number panel, crossed loop, and runic text on the complete original sheet.]
LP2-15: the number panel, crossed loop, and runic text on the complete original sheet. Page record · Original JPEG
What the drawing shows
The two lobes cross, but their outlines have visible openings. The recorded inspection describes an open-loop drawing. “Infinity sign” is a useful way to find it; it does not establish an exact Unicode symbol or a number encoded by that symbol.
A Möbius strip is a surface made by joining the ends of a strip with a half-twist. An infinity sign is a two-dimensional figure-eight shape. Those are different objects: a crossed outline alone cannot demonstrate that a surface has a half-twist. A proposed Möbius interpretation needs to specify how the page’s lines, crossings, and gaps encode that surface.
The name also belongs to the Möbius function μ(n), an arithmetic rule based on prime factors. Its outputs are −1, 0 and 1. The linked guide explains that meaning separately; the drawing and the word MOBIUS do not establish that this function is the intended cipher operation.
Pages in the community grouping
The grouping runs from LP2-15 through LP2-22. It does not mean that every sheet contains the same motif, or that all eight use the same cipher. Select any preview to inspect that page’s record.
[Image: LP2-15 manuscript preview]
LP2-15 · Read
[Image: LP2-16 manuscript preview]

LP2-17 · Read

LP2-18 · Read
[Image: LP2-19 manuscript preview]

[Image: LP2-21 manuscript preview]
LP2-21 · Read
[Image: LP2-22 manuscript preview]
LP2-22 · Read
The text-only middle pages
LP2-17–21 each contain twelve rows of black runes within broad blank margins. The crossed-loop drawing on LP2-15 is not repeated on these sheets. Their page records now include regions you can open in the image inspector: 17, 18, 19, 20, and 21.
A spacing difference on LP2-21
On LP2-21, a wider gap separates the second and third rows. That is a layout observation, not a decoded paragraph break. If you test a rule that resets at this gap, record the reset as an assumption and compare its result with the same rule without the reset.
[Image: First three rows of LP2-21, showing the wider gap after row two.]
Upper text block of LP2-21. Compare the spacing between the first two rows with the gap before the third. Read the full sheet · Original JPEG.
Punctuation is a separate layer
Small dots and compact dotted clusters occur among the runes and sometimes at the start of a row. Examples include the start of row three on LP2-19 and row seven on LP2-20. The dots guide explains why visual marks and transcription punctuation need to be distinguished. For rune-only statistics such as index of coincidence, punctuation is excluded from the symbol counts. A study of spacing or separators needs to preserve that information separately; excluding it from one calculation does not show that it has no role.
The closing page: crossbars and a reclining figure
LP2-22 looks quite different from the opening number panel. Six rows of black runes end in a small red dotted mark. Under the text sits a dark horizontal drawing with three thick crossbars; farther down, a reclining human figure extends across the bottom edge, feet to the left and head to the right.
[Image: Lower portion of LP2-22: the dark three-crossbar drawing above a reclining human figure.]
Detail of the original LP2-22 image, from below the text to the bottom edge. Read the full page · Download the original JPEG
The figure is a useful feature to search for and compare, but an identification needs more than a resemblance. Its posture alone cannot establish a death scene, a named person, or a borrowed composition. The page record has separate inspection regions for the red mark, the crossbar drawing, and the figure.
Reclining figures also appear along the bottoms of LP1-14–16. On LP1-14, the figure sits beneath the second koan on LP1-14. On all three LP1 sheets the head is on the left and the feet on the right, opposite to LP2-22. This gives a concrete comparison across the two releases, without establishing that the images are exact reflections or that their accompanying texts share a cipher.
[Image: Bottom of LP1-14: reclining human figure with head on the left and feet on the right.]
Bottom 600 pixels of the original LP1-14 sheet. Read the full page · Original JPEG.
Even within this grouping, layouts vary. LP2-16, immediately after the panel page, has twelve rows of black text and no separate illustration. Treat the community section name as a way to locate these sheets; whether their text shares a key or transformation remains a separate question.
Following the numerical details
The panel contains sixteen numbers; 3299 is red. The panel article gives every value, row and column totals, and a reproducible calculation. For an idea involving prime positions or reversed digits, use prime indices and emirps before assigning those operations to the drawing.
There is also a literal MOBIUS in the known Some Wisdom reading. That textual occurrence is a separate piece of evidence. A shared name is a reason to compare the pages, not proof that one supplies a key for the other.

Cuneiform-like mark

Compare the repeated mark on LP2-33–39, including its different placement on the first page.

A compact, two-row mark repeats on LP2-33–39. It is commonly called the cuneiform mark. The visible mark belongs in an illustrated index even though its intended meaning is not established.
[Image: Two-row cuneiform-like mark from LP2-33, displayed in its original orientation]
LP2-33 · Below the runic text. Cropped view of the original; no rotation or reflection. Complete sheet · Original JPEG
[Image: Two-row cuneiform-like mark from LP2-34, displayed in its original orientation]
LP2-34 · Above the runic text. Cropped view of the original; no rotation or reflection. Complete sheet · Original JPEG
Where to find it
Placement matters. On LP2-33 the mark is at the bottom; on LP2-34–39 it is above the main text. Calling it a “header” without that exception would hide a potentially relevant layout difference. The previews below let you compare all seven sheets.
[Image: LP2-33 manuscript preview]
LP2-33 · Read
[Image: LP2-34 manuscript preview]
LP2-34 · Read
[Image: LP2-35 manuscript preview]
LP2-35 · Read
[Image: LP2-36 manuscript preview]
LP2-36 · Read
[Image: LP2-37 manuscript preview]
LP2-37 · Read
[Image: LP2-38 manuscript preview]
LP2-38 · Read
[Image: LP2-39 manuscript preview]
LP2-39 · Read
What the name tells us
The British Museum’s Mesopotamia guide explains how early pictograms developed into wedge-shaped writing called cuneiform. Here it is the community’s name for a visual resemblance. Identifying the manuscript mark as a particular historical sign would require a sign-by-sign comparison with a specified script, period, orientation, and reading. The label alone is not a translation.
The repeated motif is also not part of the ordinary 29-rune Gematria Primus alphabet. Do not assign it a rune index or prime value merely because it occurs beside runic text.
Is cuneiform a language?

Cuneiform is a writing system, not the name of one language. Sumerian, Akkadian, and Hittite were among the languages written with it. Oxford’s Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature explains that signs could represent words (logograms) or sounds, including syllables (phonograms). A sign could have several reading values; surrounding language and context help determine which one applies.

That distinction matters when investigating this manuscript. Even a convincing match to a historical sign would leave questions about its reading and use here. “It resembles cuneiform” does not tell us whether the mark represents a word, a sound, a decorative motif, or an instruction.

From resemblance to a proposed reading

The following steps separate claims that are easy to blur together. They are a way to document a comparison, not a decipherment of the mark.

	Claim	What to show

	Visual resemblance	Place the manuscript detail beside the proposed comparison. Preserve orientation and show every rotation or reflection you introduce.

	Historical sign identification	Cite a sign list or documented inscription, its date and writing tradition. Explain both matching features and differences.

	Chosen reading	State the language and reading value you select. Explain why you choose it over alternatives.

	Use in Liber Primus	Show how the proposed reading relates to the surrounding page. A historical meaning alone does not establish the puzzle’s intended use.


Transliteration records a reading in another writing system; translation expresses meaning in another language. Neither is simply tracing the wedges. In Liberpedia’s transcription guide, the immediate task is more limited: record what is visibly present before interpreting it. Keep a proposed reading separate from that record, and describe any test using the experiment documentation guide.

Reading a sign list’s notation

A number in a scholarly label need not be a number written in the ancient text. Oxford’s ETCSL introduction explains these conventions:

	Notation or term	What it distinguishes

	gu, gu₂, gu₃	Different signs sharing a phonetic value: homophony. The subscripts distinguish readings; they are not quantities.

	Determinative	A category marker, such as one preceding a deity’s name. Such markers are thought to have been unpronounced.

	Superscript	One way ETCSL displays a determinative in transliteration.


When recording a proposed comparison, preserve the source’s notation and explain it. Do not automatically treat its subscript as a cipher digit, an exponent or a Gematria Primus value. This glossary does not identify any of those signs in the Liber Primus motif.

Other details in this section
LP2-33 and LP2-39 show conspicuous separated black dots. LP2-36–38 include red decimal labels: 1 on page 36, 2–4 on page 37, and 5 on page 38. These observations help locate parts of the section; they do not establish what a dot or label instructs the reader to do. See dots and punctuation for the distinction between printed shapes and transcription notation.
Follow the red numbers across pages

	Page	Visible decimal labels	Placement

	LP2-36	1	At the start of a block below the opening text.

	LP2-37	2, 3, 4	At successive block starts, from top to bottom.

	LP2-38	5	Below the opening block, which has no new decimal label.


This sequence is useful for recording layout before testing a method. A page break, a new text block, and a printed number are separate observations. If you propose restarting a key at one of them, say which one and record its exact rune position. The visual sequence alone does not tell us whether any key should restart. See key advancement and counting conventions and red text and color boundaries.

Are the repeated marks identical?

The six windows on LP2-34–39 have exactly the same decoded RGB pixels. The LP2-33 window differs from each of them at 43,601 of 184,800 pixel positions. This is a comparison of fixed rectangles in the archived originals, including their surrounding whitespace.

	Comparison	Pairs checked	Result

	Every pair among LP2-34–39	15	All corresponding RGB values equal.

	LP2-33 against each of LP2-34–39	6	43,601 differing pixels in each comparison.


A pixel counts as different when at least one of its red, green or blue channel values differs. There is no tolerance, rotation, reflection, resizing or search for a better alignment. All seven complete JPEG files have different SHA-256 hashes: equal decoded windows do not mean identical page files.

The exact windows

Each rectangle is 420 × 440 pixels in a 2400 × 3600 original. Coordinates start at the upper-left corner; x increases rightward and y downward. Right and bottom bounds are excluded, following the image-region convention. The two enlarged details at the top of this guide show these windows on pages 33 and 34.

	Pages	Left, top	Right, bottom	Position

	LP2-33	1000, 3030	1420, 3470	Below the text

	LP2-34–39	1000, 130	1420, 570	Above the text


These are comparison windows, not measurements of the exact ink boundary. Their coordinates were chosen after visual inspection, and preliminary equality was observed before the report script was written. This is a descriptive measurement, not a statistical test of an independently selected hypothesis.

Repeat the pixel comparison

Download the reference-data ZIP and original-images ZIP. Extract both into the same folder, preserving their directories. The script needs Python 3 and Pillow; see running the reproduction scripts for setup help. Run these commands from that folder:

python -m pip install Pillow
python scripts/measure_cuneiform_windows.py --check

The check decodes the seven original JPEGs, compares all 21 pairs, and checks the source-file hashes and measured results against the saved report. It prints PASS only when they agree. It does not modify the images.

Inspect or download the complete comparison report (JSON) and measurement script. The report records every rectangle, source hash, decoded-window hash, differing-pixel count and maximum channel difference. To save a new report without replacing the reference:

python scripts/measure_cuneiform_windows.py --output my-cuneiform-comparison.json

The recorded decoder was Pillow 11.3.0 with JPEG codec 8.0. A different version is allowed, but any changed decoded pixels or original-file hashes will fail the check. If that happens, compare decoder versions and verify the downloaded files before interpreting it as a manuscript difference.

What the equality tells us

The six upper-page windows share the same decoded pixel content in this archive. That is stronger than saying they look similar, but it does not identify a historical sign, translate it, or establish how the pages were constructed. The unequal LP2-33 window also does not prove a different sign: placement, surrounding pixels, compression or small visual changes can affect an exact comparison.

No alignment search or comparison outside these rectangles was performed. A claim about the whole motif, its origin or its meaning needs additional evidence. Keep such proposals separate from this repeatable image measurement.

Spirals and branching borders

Compare the curled borders on LP2-03–07 with the branching designs on LP2-40–55, and plan a measurable geometric comparison.

Several groups of Liber Primus pages have curled drawings beside the text. The community calls LP2-03–07 “Spirals,” LP2-40–53 “Spiral Branches,” and LP2-54–55 “Spiral & Dead Tree.” These names make the images easier to find. Comparing their actual linework is more useful than treating every curl as the same symbol.
The curled borders on LP2-03–07
On LP2-03, paired curves frame the left and right margins of the runic text. Each side has a tighter upper curl and a longer lower curve. LP2-07 retains this border arrangement, while its lower text ends above a red line and five large black dots.
[Image: LP2-03 cropped page preview]
LP2-03 · Read
[Image: LP2-07 cropped page preview]
LP2-07 · Read
The dots are a separate feature from the small groups of specks beside the upper curls. See dots and punctuation for examples of why position, size, and arrangement should be recorded separately.
Open the intervening pages: LP2-04 · LP2-05 · LP2-06.
The branching borders on LP2-40–55
LP2-40 has curls joined to branching, root-like forms on both sides of the text. LP2-53 shows a winged insect below its red closing passage. The next pair, LP2-54–55, continues the branching border style; LP2-55 also contains a pale tree-shaped drawing above a winged insect.
[Image: LP2-40 cropped page preview]
LP2-40 · Read
[Image: LP2-53 cropped page preview]
LP2-53 · Read
[Image: LP2-54 cropped page preview]
LP2-54 · Read
[Image: LP2-55 cropped page preview]
LP2-55 · Read
Use the illustrated index to inspect the intervening LP2-40–53 pages. The branches and trees article compares these forms with the narrow branching drawing on LP2-08–14.
Compare the group openings: LP2-40 and LP2-54

Both pages begin with an enlarged red rune beside three rows and smaller red text at the start of the first row. On LP2-54, the red opening ends with a compact punctuation cluster before the black runes continue. The shared border style does not erase these differences in text and punctuation.

Each page also has a small cluster beside the inner edge of each border. On the left, three marks are solid black and two are pale ring outlines; on the right, all five are solid. The same fill pattern is recorded on LP2-53, with enlarged views. This comparison covers these inspected pages, not every intervening page.

Open the LP2-40 observations or LP2-54 observations beside the original images. The pale tree and winged figure that explain the community name “Spiral & Dead Tree” are on LP2-55; the name does not mean both pages contain a tree.

A useful comparison starts with a question
	Question	What to record	What the result would establish
	Do two pages reuse the same border?	Original-file hashes, crop rectangles, alignment, and pixel differences	Agreement under the stated alignment and tolerance
	Are the two margins mirror images?	A defined reflection axis and corresponding points on both drawings	How closely the selected regions match after reflection
	Does a curl follow a particular spiral?	A centre, sampled points, coordinate scale, fitted parameters, and residuals	The quality of that geometric fit, compared with alternatives
For example, a logarithmic spiral has r = a exp(bθ), while an Archimedean spiral has r = a + bθ. Here r is distance from the chosen centre and θ is angle. Merely seeing a curl does not select either model. The chosen centre and the thickness of the drawn line can strongly affect a fit.
Before connecting geometry to a cipher, state how a measured result would change the decoding operation. “The borders look symmetric” and “read alternate lines backwards” are separate claims; the first does not supply the second without an explicit rule.
Preparing a reproducible image comparison
Choose the pages and the feature before fitting anything. Include a comparison page with a visibly different border.
Download the original files and verify their SHA-256 hashes.
Record rectangles using original-image coordinates. Keep the original pixels and any transformed comparison image separately.
Document scaling, rotation, reflection, thresholding, and the score used to compare the shapes.
Publish the script and output together, including mismatches. A visually plausible overlay alone is not enough to reproduce the comparison.
This article provides an inspection route and a comparison method. It does not report a completed geometric fit or establish a cipher role for the borders.

Branches and trees

Locate the narrow branching drawings on LP2-08–14 and the pale tree on LP2-55; distinguish tips, junctions, and segments before counting.

Branching forms occur in both releases. They differ in placement and appearance: a narrow drawing beside the text on LP2-08–14, curled borders later in the manuscript, and a pale tree-shaped drawing inside LP2-55. Keeping these examples separate makes it possible to compare them without losing their page context.
The leafy border on the Welcome pages
LP1-03 and LP1-04 place their text inside thick curving branches, with dense leaf shapes above and more open loops along the sides. Branches turn inward beneath the text. The broad arrangement is shared across the two sheets; describing that resemblance is not a pixel-level claim that every line is identical.
[Image: Top of LP1-03: thick branches and dense leaf-shaped forms meet above the text column.]
Top 650 pixels of LP1-03. Complete page · Original JPEG.
The Welcome reading spans both pages. Its language of pilgrimage and emergence gives textual context, but does not identify the plant forms or establish that the border encodes a route. Compare these enclosing branches with the separate margin drawing on LP2-08–14 below.
The small instruction at the bottom of LP1-04
Just above the lower border, LP1-04 has a line of red runes much smaller than the main writing. The known reading gives AN INSTRUCTIAN. COMMAND YOUR OWN SELF. This is visible text on the page, not an extracted hidden message.
[Image: LP1-04 detail: the small red runic instruction below the main passage.]
Original-image detail, rectangle [800, 2920, 800, 100]. Complete page · Original JPEG.
Use the complete reading and reproduction instructions to check how the line is decoded. Keeping it with the preceding text avoids losing a short instruction simply because it falls outside the main block. The comparison of self-direction instructions places this sentence beside LP1-13 and LP1-16. The red-writing guide explains why color and placement should be recorded separately from rune values.
The narrow branching drawing on LP2-08–14
LP2-08 shows a long, slender form along the left margin. Smaller lines branch off toward its upper and lower ends, while the main text sits to its right. LP2-14 shows the same broad arrangement and includes an insect drawing below the text at the right.
[Image: LP2-08 cropped page preview]
LP2-08 · Read
[Image: LP2-14 cropped page preview]
LP2-14 · Read
The community groups LP2-08–14 under “Branches.” Open the middle pages to compare placement and linework: 09 · 10 · 11 · 12 · 13. The group name does not establish that the form represents a particular plant species, diagram, or cipher key.
The branch changes sides on successive pages

Across this seven-page group, the branch alternates between the left and right margins. Read the sequence in archive order:

	Branch position	Pages

	Left of the text	08, 10, 12, 14

	Right of the text	09, 11, 13


[Image: LP2-08 with the branch to the left of the rune column]
LP2-08: left margin.
[Image: LP2-09 with the branch to the right of the rune column]
LP2-09: right margin.

A drawing can move to the other margin without being mirrored. To test reflection, compare corresponding tips, junctions, and bends after aligning the images; the left/right sequence alone does not answer that question. Likewise, a proposal to reverse text on alternating pages would be an additional operation to test, not something already demonstrated by this layout.

Curled borders and the pale tree
On LP2-40, branching forms are part of the curled drawings on both sides of the text. LP2-55 has that border style as well as a much lighter tree-shaped drawing in the central space above the insect. Its low contrast is itself a reason to consult the original image rather than relying on a transcription.
[Image: LP2-40 cropped page preview]
LP2-40 · Read
[Image: LP2-55 cropped page preview]
LP2-55 · Read
Compare the spiral and branching borders, or use the illustrated index to browse the other artwork groups, including the separately named LP2-27–32 “Wing & Tree” group.
The Wing and Tree group adds another distinct example: the soft-edged tree-shaped figure on LP2-32. It should not be conflated with the pale, more finely outlined drawing on LP2-55.
[Image: LP2-32: soft-edged tree-shaped drawing]
LP2-32 — soft-edged tree-shaped drawing. Open reader
Compare the two central tree drawings
These close views use equally wide regions of the original images. LP2-32 has broad, dark forms with soft edges. LP2-55 has much lighter, outlined contours with enclosed white spaces. The difference is already present in the preserved JPEGs; neither view has been sharpened or given extra contrast.
[Image: LP2-32: dark, soft-edged drawing in an unenhanced original-image detail.]
LP2-32: dark, soft-edged drawing. Full page.
[Image: LP2-55: pale, outlined drawing in an unenhanced original-image detail.]
LP2-55: pale, outlined drawing. Full page.
Both drawings have a trunk-like base and branching forms, but that resemblance does not yet establish reuse of one image. A proposed match needs corresponding bends, junctions, and proportions, with any transformations stated. Nor can this comparison tell us why one drawing is faint or the other soft-edged.
The page records offer an Inspect control for each tree. The selected rectangles are [650, 2050, 1100, 1150] on LP2-32 and [650, 1400, 1100, 1100] on LP2-55, in original-image pixels. They locate the drawings for inspection; they are not branch-count measurements.
What does “count the branches” mean?
A branch count sounds straightforward until two people trace the same drawing differently. One may count every visible line leaving a trunk; another may count terminal tips; a third may count each segment between junctions. Those are different measurements.
	Quantity	A possible explicit definition
	Tips	Endpoints of a traced line, excluding the boundary of the chosen crop
	Junctions	Locations where three or more traced segments meet
	Segments	Paths between tips or junctions, with no junction in their interior
	Main stem	A selected path identified by its endpoints and a stated selection rule
Under a graph representation, tips and junctions become vertices and the connecting segments become edges. A visually tree-like drawing need not yield a mathematical tree: a crossing may or may not be a connection, and a closed loop would change the graph. Publish an annotated tracing so another person can see those choices.
Handling the pale drawing on LP2-55
Increasing contrast can make a faint line easier to see, but it also changes the displayed pixels. Preserve the original file, label an enhanced image as a derivative, and record the operation. If a claim depends on a feature visible only after enhancement, show the corresponding unmodified region too.
For numerical work, choose the brightness threshold before counting and check how modest changes affect the result. A count that changes sharply with the threshold needs that sensitivity reported. The existing image-region guide explains thresholds used for other published measurements; those settings have not been validated as a segmentation method for this pale tree.
From appearance to interpretation
A botanical identification, a religious association, and a decoding instruction each require different evidence. A comparison with a named artwork should show the proposed source image and the matching features. A cipher proposal should specify how the drawing produces an ordered sequence or operation, rather than selecting a count because it happens to fit.
For wider interpretation, start with philosophical themes in the known readings. That article distinguishes what the text says from suggested connections. No particular symbolic meaning is assigned to these branching drawings here.
Paired plant borders on LP2-41–44
These four sheets each have twelve rows of black runes between tall curling stems. Look for the drooping narrow leaves, the root-like lower branches, and the groups of filled dots beside the stems. The page records provide original-image inspection regions: 41, 42, 43, and 44.
[Image: Plant borders flanking the runic text on LP2-41, with curled tips, drooping leaves, filled dots, and branching bases.]
Paired borders of LP2-41, original-image region [0, 760, 2400, 2100]. Complete sheet · Original JPEG.
A related border arrangement also frames the alphanumeric grids on LP2-49–51. This gives a visual comparison across different text layouts. It does not by itself establish identical artwork files, a plant species, or a shared cipher.
Keep the border dots separate from marks within the text. LP2-42 has paired short vertical strokes near the right ends of rows three and six; LP2-43 has a pair near the end of row one. Those observations are recorded on the individual pages. Their resemblance to familiar punctuation is not enough to assign a grammatical role; the punctuation guide explains how to preserve visual distinctions in an analysis.
The runic pages around the grids
The same broad border arrangement continues on LP2-45, 46, 47, and 48. Each has twelve runic rows. LP2-49–51 then place alphanumeric arrays inside the borders, before LP2-52 returns to a full twelve-row runic block.
	Pages	Central content
	LP2-45–48	Twelve runic rows on each sheet
	LP2-49–51	Alphanumeric grids; runic text above the first and below the last
	LP2-52	Twelve runic rows
That sequence is useful when defining a test's scope. A proposal based on the grid entries should say whether it also uses the surrounding runes or border marks. The change in central content does not by itself demonstrate a new key, cipher, or instruction to reset an operation.
There are also smaller differences worth inspecting. LP2-47 ends its first row with a dotted cluster. On LP2-48, small dots precede the first runes of rows four and six. The page records locate these examples in the originals; neither their placement nor the shared border assigns them a decoded meaning.
